events.excerpt: Hello everyone, I am an engineer on the sBTC team at Stacks Labs. We are making some changes to the sBTC protocol that may be relevant to you. Changes like this are made on a regular basis to bring you ongoing improvement of the protocol’s security. 1. A new deposit format is live The sBTC signers and Emily support a new deposit format that you can start testing on mainnet today. The new deposit format, v2, improves the security of the sBTC protocol. Specifically, new deposits are locked with a standard Bitcoin multisig, which Bitcoin enforces directly. The old deposit format, v1, depended on an aggregate key from a custom threshold-signature protocol. Moving to the new format allows us to remove that complex cryptography from what secures deposits. However, this new format will increase the weight on Bitcoin by about 4x compared to the old format. This means the assessed Bitcoin fees are about 4 times higher than they are now. Once we ship the changes described in section 3, the extra weight will raise the Bitcoin fee paid by both deposit and withdrawal requests. events.excerpt: Hi everyone. I’m Leandro, a full-stack developer and open-source contributor with experience in AI, blockchain, web and mobile development, and developer tooling. I recently submitted a grant proposal for Zcash Wallet Devtools , an open-source toolkit designed to improve the developer experience when building applications with Zcash. What’s the idea? Integrating Zcash wallets and payment requests into web applications can be challenging to debug. Developers often need to rely on console logs, manually inspect SDK responses, and troubleshoot different wallet behaviors. I’d like to make that process easier by building a lightweight, privacy-aware debugging toolkit inspired by tools like React Query Devtools and Solana’s Connector Debugger. What will it include? TypeScript SDK: Instrumentation for wallet connections, events, state changes, and errors. Interactive Devtools Dashboard: A visual panel that runs inside applications during development. ZIP-321 Diagnostics: Inspect payment request lifecycle events and troubleshoot integration issues. Privacy-Aware Logging: Protect sensitive wallet information by default. Wallet Integration: Initial support for one compatible Zcash wallet SDK. Next.js Demo: A working example showing how everything integrates. Bilingual Documentation: Techni
events.headline: Zcash Wallet Devtools - Privacy-Aware Debugging Toolkit for Web Developers

events.excerpt: ERC-3668 (CCIP-Read) lets a contract hand a read off to a gateway, but the gateway either has to be trusted or has to return a proof the contract can verify. For many cross-chain reads a valid proof cannot be produced. That does not make the read unsafe, because the client usually already trusts its own RPC connection to the other chain and could simply make the call itself. ERC-8446 lets the client act as the gateway. The contract reverts with OffchainLookup as usual, with an x-chain URL that names the chain and contract to read, and the client calls that contract with its own RPC and passes the result to the callback exactly as eth_call returns it. No third party is involved. The chain and address are encoded as an ERC-7930 Interoperable Address, for example USDC on Base. x-chain:0x0001000002210514833589fcd6edb6e08f4c7c32d4f71b54bda02913 An optional ?finalized=true makes the read at the finalized block instead of the latest one. The client alone decides whether it can safely read a given chain, and never takes RPC endpoints from the contract. Nested x-chain lookups are not followed, so each call makes at most one cross-chain hop. Contracts can also tell when a client does not support the ERC. They add a data: URL after the x-chain URL, which only older clients reach, and it del
events.headline: ERC-8446: Cross-Chain Client Gateway for CCIP-Read

events.excerpt: ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 store metadata onchain as key-value pairs, but a JSON document has no compact way to point at those values. A URL that names the contract, the chain, and the token ID repeats what the client already knows and differs for every token. ERC-8493 defines the onchain URI scheme. The contract and token ID are not written in the URI, they come from the function that returned the document. { "image": "onchain:image/png", "thumbnail": { "small": "onchain:image/png?key=thumb.small" } } onchain:image/png is 17 bytes and works unchanged for every token. When the URI comes from tokenURI or uri , the client reads it with metadata(tokenId, key) from ERC-8048, and when it comes from contractURI , with metadata(key) from ERC-8049. A direct member of the top-level document uses its own name as the key, and everywhere else the key parameter names it. Tokens that are already deployed can use the scheme by adding a metadata_contract property to their JSON, which points the client at a separate metadata contract. Linked JSON documents keep the same contract and token, so the whole thing reads as one data tree. The scheme adds no contract surface. Existing ERC-8048 and ERC-8049 contracts support it with no change, and a client that does not know the scheme sees a URI it can ignore
events.headline: ERC-8493: Onchain URI Scheme

events.excerpt: The image of the red ring around the black hole M87, produced by the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) array, made front-page news around the world in 2019. There was one problem: there was a slim chance the depiction might be wrong. This week, a small team of four Australian researchers have published their work confirming the result based on a new machine learning algorithm using the same base data. The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image came from hundreds of scientists working together to capture the first direct view of a black hole's shadow. The measurements were taken at eight telescopes around the world, at locations including Chile, the US, and Antarctica. Reconstructing the image from the data so geographically distant meant instrument and environment errors could influence the accuracy of the resulting image. Potentially, alternative analyses of the data could have reconstructed an image without the iconic ring shape. Samuel Lai – a postdoctoral fellow at the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO) in Western Australia – and his team created an independent imaging algorithm to process the historic dataset to validate the result. events.excerpt: The CNCF End User Community is launching its User Group Program at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America. These are long-lived groups, each built around an industry vertical or problem domain, that serves the common need of the end user community, and reports directly to the CNCF Technical Advisory Board (TAB). Why user groups Cloud native adoption looks different in a telecom network, a research lab, a public agency and a platform team at a software company. Each has its own constraints, vocabulary and gaps in the tooling landscape. A CNCF User Group gives each of those communities a durable place to organize around its own needs, rather than relying on one-off efforts that fade after a single project or event. A User Group is the primary organizational unit of the program. It is aligned with an industry vertical, a problem domain, or a common need of the CNCF end user community, and it is long-lived by design: user groups perform standing functions for projects and the organizations that adopt them. Each group: Represents and serves the needs of end users in its domain Identifies gaps in the CNCF project portfolio and helps attract projects to fill them Educates users with unbiased, practical information scoped to cloud native Proposes community-sourced reference architectures
events.headline: Introducing CNCF User Groups: Long-lived homes for End User collaboration

events.excerpt: What OpenShell is AI agents do more than call APIs. They run shells, install packages, read files, and open network connections. Often they act on text they pulled from the internet a minute earlier. So every agent is untrusted code that holds real credentials. OpenShell , started by NVIDIA and now a CNCF Sandbox project , is a runtime for running agents like this safely. OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox. A trusted supervisor outside the sandbox decides what the agent may reach. You declare four kinds of control in YAML: Filesystem : Landlock limits which paths the agent can read or write. In the demo, /usr, /etc, and a few other paths are read-only, and only /sandbox, /tmp, and /dev/null are writable. Process : before the agent starts, the sandbox runtime drops it to a non-root user with no capabilities and applies seccomp. Network : outbound traffic is denied by default. Rules can allow traffic per binary, host, port, and HTTP method. Credentials : the agent sees only a placeholder for each API key. The supervisor swaps in the real key, and only for endpoints the provider allows. For Kubernetes admins, a key point is that OpenShell does not bring its own scheduler. Its Kubernetes backend uses Agent Sandbox , the agents.x-k8s.io Sandbox resource from SIG Apps. Agents show

events.excerpt: Cloudflare recently announced Meerkat , an experimental distributed consensus service designed to manage our internal global control plane. It is powered by a new consensus algorithm published by researchers Tennage & Băsescu et al. called QuePaxa (2023). QuePaxa is an unusual choice; most consensus systems use well-established consensus algorithms like Raft, (Multi-)Paxos or Viewstamped Replication. These algorithms are well understood, have mature implementations, and usually work well. Unfortunately, common consensus algorithms often suffer in wide-area networks with volatile network connectivity and latency, i.e., networks like the Internet, which is where Meerkat runs. These algorithms rely on a single leader process being available and having predictable latency. If the leader goes down, experiences higher latency than usual, or is disconnected, the entire consensus system slows down or becomes unavailable until the leader is replaced. This is unacceptable for Meerkat. Meerkat’s global deployment environment led us to a newer consensus algorithm, QuePaxa, which promises better stability despite volatility, in large part by not relying on a leader to make progress. In this post we’ll explain why we chose QuePaxa and how the QuePaxa algorithm works. What we’re building and wh
events.headline: Choosing QuePaxa, an unusual consensus algorithm

events.excerpt: Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky. The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set. "Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18. For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website. According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present. Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured. events.headline: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away

events.excerpt: A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes. Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum. You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated. YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data. The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses. events.headline: 2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials

"The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. events.excerpt: Even my family thinks I’m a little robotic. Logical, linear, sequential, methodical. But hey, I’m an engineer, and that’s part of what makes me good at my job. If I were operating on the same volatile cocktail of emotions, knee-jerk reactions, and intuition that most people operate on, I wouldn’t have been nearly as effective building enterprise software architecture at Disney, Dell, SAP, VMware, and now Control Plane. Worse yet, I might have had to become a marketer, or a designer, or a human resources specialist…or even a salesperson. Not very long ago (in 2024, and for fifty years before that), software engineers like me were the best robots anyone had access to. The CIO at Disney would ask me to redesign FastPass from the ground up, and I would do it in one long-running process over a weekend while he sipped coffee and watched the game. The head of Dell’s Identity Management business would bring me a huge project, and I would dive in, writing thousands of lines of code by hand. And even though I was pretty consistent and logical, and so were (most of) my engineering colleagues, things could get messy fast. events.excerpt: The following is an opinion post reflecting my vision for a possible design direction for Ethereum, not a concrete design. What I argue for is to rethink the notions of scaling, availability, and finality according to the principles of elasticity. TL;DR Ethereum’s capacity is configured in advance: one block per slot, a fixed slot time, a gas limit and a size limit. Price matches demand to it, and safety margins cover for the network. No protocol-wide rule adapts capacity limits to measured resource pressure. Elasticity is first of all about robustness. An elastic system measures what it can carry and takes on less when it is falling behind. A system without that feedback is the kind that goes into congestion collapse, and Ethereum’s overload incidents look like it. Scaling comes with it. A system that can back off can afford to run close to what the network and the nodes can carry, where a fixed margin has to pay for the worst day every day. TCP is the working example: its congestion control was built to stop collapses, and it is also much of why the same protocol, with small changes, runs on modems and on fibre. events.excerpt: "Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work. Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors. The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE , short for the XLA Serving Engine. One-shot inference XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang ), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google. "LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach , Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday. At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search. These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on
events.headline: Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python

events.excerpt: Hi all, If you work with more than one Cosmos chain, you’ve probably hit this: chain binaries don’t update themselves. After a network upgrade, the gaiad or osmosisd on your machine quietly goes stale, and you find out when a transaction fails or a query returns something odd. Cosmovisor solves this for running nodes, but nothing did for developers, CLI users and CI. I built cosmup to fill that gap. It’s a small Go CLI that reads the Cosmos chain registry, downloads the right binary for your platform, verifies its SHA256, and keeps versions side by side. $ cosmup check osmosis Local: v30.0.0 (/usr/local/bin/osmosisd) Network: v31.0.0 (via https://lcd.osmosis.zone) Status: does not match the network; run: cosmup install osmosis@v31.0.0 $ cosmup install osmosis Verified sha256 d435408b... Active: osmosis v31.0.0 What it does: install / use / list: install any version listed in the chain registry, switch between installed versions instantly check: compares your local binary with the version the live network runs, and shows scheduled upgrades (exits 1 on mismatch, so it works in CI) update: moves every installed chain to its recommended version cosmovisor: for validators, puts a verified upgrade binary into cosmovisor’s upgrades folder ahead of the upgrade height remove / prune: clea
events.headline: Cosmup: install, switch and check Cosmos chain binaries (like nvm, for gaiad/osmosisd/...)

events.excerpt: UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better. Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem. There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd , an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT . Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear. Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands. The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery. Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap –
events.headline: Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens
